title: Play Maelstrom Online — Ambrosia's Mac Classic, Free & Legal
description: Maelstrom, the Asteroids game that made Ambrosia Software, running free in your browser. GPL engine, Creative Commons artwork, nothing to install.
keywords: maelstrom game, play maelstrom online, ambrosia software maelstrom, maelstrom mac, asteroids mac game, andrew welch maelstrom
ogDescription: Ambrosia's Asteroids, free and legal, booting straight into the game on an emulated Macintosh.
h1: Maelstrom — Asteroids, taken far too seriously
author: Ambrosia Software
fullyFree: Ambrosia's own licence permits non-profit redistribution, and the company later released the engine under the GPL and the artwork under Creative Commons. The whole game is here — no crippled demo, no level lock.
licenseReason: Maelstrom shipped as shareware, and shareware was designed to be copied. The licence file on this very disk says non-profit distribution is acceptable without asking, provided the software is unmodified and complete — which is why the registration notice you see on startup is still there, untouched. Ambrosia went further later: the engine became GPL in 1999 and the artwork Creative Commons in 2010. Full provenance is in notices/maelstrom.md.
intro:
In 1992 a Macintosh shareware author decided that Asteroids deserved better, and spent an unreasonable amount of effort proving it. Maelstrom has rendered 3D rock sprites, a proper soundtrack, screen-shaking explosions, power-ups, and a sense of weight that the 1979 original never had. It is still, more than thirty years on, one of the best arcade games written for any Macintosh.

It boots straight into the game here, with nothing to install. Ambrosia later released the engine under the GPL and the artwork under Creative Commons, which is why it can be here at all — though the 1990s build you are playing still opens with the shareware notice it shipped with. Click Not Yet and play.
launchNote: Boots straight into Maelstrom. The first thing you see is Ambrosia’s 1990s shareware notice — click “Not Yet”, then press a key to play.

sections.h: How it works & what to expect
sections.html:
MachineMacintosh IIfx, 32 MB RAM, 640×480
SystemSystem 7.5.3
EmulatorBasilisk II, compiled to WebAssembly
VersionMaelstrom 1.4.3, the last Macintosh release
SoundYes, and it matters. Click inside the screen once — browsers block audio until you do.
MobileIt runs, but this is a keyboard game. Use a real keyboard.

The machine takes about half a minute to start and opens the Maelstrom folder on the desktop; double-click Maelstrom to play. If the keys do nothing, click once on the game screen — the browser gives it the keyboard only after you have interacted with it.

Maelstrom's own Preferences dialog lists every key and lets you change them, which is worth doing if the defaults fight your keyboard.

sections.h: What makes it more than a clone
sections.html:
The rocks are the giveaway. They are not vector outlines or flat polygons; they are pre-rendered 3D objects, tumbling in animation frames, and in 1992 on a Macintosh that was showing off. Shoot one and it breaks into smaller ones that are also properly rendered, and the screen jolts.

On top of that sits everything Asteroids did not have. Power-ups drift down and change your ship: multiple shots, autofire, shields, extra lives. Enemy ships arrive and actually aim. There are bonus levels. There is a two-player mode over AppleTalk, which is not much use here. And there is a high score table that Ambrosia ran as a genuine worldwide contest, which is the sort of thing a shareware author did when the alternative was nothing.

It is also hard in the way arcade games were hard: not unfair, but not interested in whether you are having a nice time.

sections.h: Why this game matters beyond the Mac
sections.html:
Maelstrom is the reason SDL exists.

In 1995 Ambrosia gave the source to Sam Lantinga, who wanted to port it to Linux. The cross-platform layer he wrote to do that became the Simple DirectMedia Layer — the library that now underpins an enormous amount of game development, from indie projects to the Steam client and countless commercial ports. It started as scaffolding to get a Macintosh Asteroids game running on X11.

Ambrosia Software itself was one of the great shareware houses: Maelstrom, Escape Velocity, Apeiron, SketchFighter, and a registration system built on trust and good jokes. You can still see that model working in the notice this build opens with — pay if you keep playing, on your honour. The company wound down in the 2010s, but Maelstrom was set free first: GPL for the code in 1999, Creative Commons for the art in 2010.

If you want to play it at a modern resolution on a modern machine, the SDL port is maintained and packaged nearly everywhere. What is here is the 1990s Macintosh build, in its own habitat.

faq.q: The game says Maelstrom is not a free product. Should it be here?
faq.a: Yes, and by Ambrosia's own rules. That notice is the shareware pitch it shipped with in the 1990s: try it, and pay if you keep playing. Shareware was built to be passed around, and the licence file on this disk says non-profit distribution is acceptable without asking, so long as nothing is modified and the complete package is included. Both conditions hold here — the notice is deliberately left intact rather than patched out. Ambrosia also released the engine under the GPL in 1999 and the artwork under Creative Commons in 2010.

faq.q: Is it legal to have this here?
faq.a: Yes. The engine is GPL and the artwork is Creative Commons Attribution, both by the decision of the people who made them. That is a firmer footing than most things preserved from this era, which survive only because nobody is left to object.

faq.q: Do I need to install anything?
faq.a: No. The emulator is WebAssembly and runs in this page. Nothing is installed and nothing is uploaded.
Click once inside the game screen. Browsers do not hand keyboard input to a page element until the visitor has interacted with it, and the same click is what unlocks the sound.
Yes — Maelstrom has a Preferences dialog that lists every key and lets you rebind it. Worth a look if the defaults are awkward on your keyboard.

faq.q: Will my high scores be saved?
faq.a: Not yet. This machine is rebuilt fresh each visit, so the score table resets. Persistent disks are on the list.

faq.q: What is the connection to SDL?
faq.a: Sam Lantinga wrote the Simple DirectMedia Layer while porting Maelstrom from the Mac to Linux in the mid-1990s. SDL went on to become one of the most widely used game libraries there is.
Maelstrom 1.4.3, the last Macintosh release, which includes the documentation and the licence text.
Yes. The SDL port is maintained and packaged for Linux, macOS and Windows, and runs at modern resolutions. This page is for the original Macintosh build.

description: Arashi, the 1993 Macintosh take on Tempest, running free in your browser. Freely distributable by its authors, source code included, nothing to install.
keywords: arashi mac game, play arashi online, tempest mac, arashi 1.1, mac shareware arcade game
ogDescription: The Mac's answer to Tempest, freely distributable, booting straight into the game.
h1: Arashi — Tempest, rebuilt for the Macintosh
author: Juri Munkki and Mike Kelly
fullyFree: The authors put the terms in one line of the ReadMe: freely distributable as long as it is not for profit. They shipped the C source with it too.
licenseReason: Arashi's ReadMe, which is on the disk you are booting, says it plainly: "ARASHI is freely distributable as long as it is not for profit." Nothing here is modified and this site carries no advertising, so both halves of that hold. The authors also included the C source, which is on the disk as they shipped it. Full provenance is in notices/arashi.md.
intro:
Atari's Tempest put you on the rim of a tube and threw things up it at you. Arashi does the same, on a Macintosh, in 1993, with colour, a soundtrack and a level compiler its authors wrote so the game could be scripted. It is faster and stranger than the original, and it has the particular quality a lot of the best Mac shareware has: someone built it because they wanted it to exist.

It boots straight into the game here. The name is Japanese for storm.
launchNote: Boots straight into Arashi's options panel. Click Start Game — or set the difficulty first.

sections.html:

SystemSystem 7.5.3

VersionArashi 1.1, June 1993 — the release with the scripting engine

MobileIt runs, but this is a mouse game and a touchscreen is a poor substitute.

Arashi needs 256 colours, which the emulated machine has. The game takes a moment to build its first level after the splash screen.

sections.h: What it added to Tempest
sections.html:
The shape is familiar: you run around the edge of a well, firing down it, while things climb up towards you. Let one reach the rim and it comes for you along it.

What Arashi adds is a decade of hardware. The wells are drawn in colour with proper shading rather than vectors. There is a soundtrack. There are power-ups, a save system, and what the ReadMe calls doomsday levels — the difficulty past the point where the game stops being reasonable.

The most interesting addition is invisible while you play. Juri Munkki wrote a game compiler and scripting language for the 1.1 release, so the levels are data rather than code. That is why the C source shipped alongside the game: the authors expected people to look.

sections.h: Mac shareware as a culture
sections.html:
Arashi is a good example of a category that barely exists now. Two people wrote an arcade game to a standard that would have been commercial a few years earlier, put it on the Info-Mac archive, asked for nothing, and included the source.

The distribution model made that normal. A shareware author had no publisher, no shelf space and no marketing, so the software had to travel by being copied — which meant the licence had to permit copying, and most of them did, in a sentence written by the author rather than a lawyer. Arashi's is one line long.

That is why a site like this can exist at all. A large part of the Macintosh catalogue between 1985 and 2000 was released on terms that explicitly allow what you are doing right now.

faq.a: Yes, on its authors' own terms. The ReadMe on the disk says it is freely distributable as long as it is not for profit. It is not a demo or a crippled version — this is the whole game.

It takes Tempest's shape and builds on it: colour, a soundtrack, power-ups, saved games, a scripting engine for the levels, and difficulty settings past anything the original attempted. Whether that makes it a clone or a successor is a matter of taste.
Effectively yes. Arashi is played by moving around the rim of the well, and it maps that to the mouse. A trackpad works; a touchscreen is a struggle.
Storm, in Japanese. The game was called something else for version 1.0 and the ReadMe notes the change in its first paragraph.

faq.q: Is the source code really included?
faq.a: It is, in a folder on the disk you are booting. The authors shipped it with the game and it has been left exactly where they put it.
Juri Munkki and Mike Kelly, released in June 1993. Munkki wrote the game compiler and scripting language for this version.

title: Play The Oregon Trail (Mac) Online — The 1991 Classroom Version
description: The Macintosh Oregon Trail, the one from the school computer lab, running in your browser. Ford the river, shoot more bison than you can carry, die of dysentery.
keywords: oregon trail online, play oregon trail, oregon trail mac, oregon trail 1991, oregon trail browser, mecc oregon trail
ogTitle: The Oregon Trail (Mac, 1991) in your browser
ogDescription: The classroom version, emulated. Choose a profession, stock up at Matt's General Store, and try to reach the Willamette Valley.
h1: The Oregon Trail on a Macintosh, in a browser tab
author: MECC
licenseReason: MECC was wound up in the late 1990s and the trail passed through The Learning Company to Houghton Mifflin Harcourt. The 1991 Macintosh release has not been sold in any form for over twenty-five years and no rights holder distributes it today. It is here because a piece of software that taught a generation to spell "dysentery" should not only exist inside a cardboard box in somebody's garage. If you hold the rights and disagree, say so and it goes within 48 hours.
intro:
Nearly everybody who sat in front of a school Macintosh between 1991 and about 1998 played this. Not the Apple II green-screen original, and not the phone remake — this one: colour, a covered wagon rolling right to left across the bottom of the screen, and a river you were never quite sure whether to ford.

It is the 1991 MECC release for the Macintosh, running here on an emulated Macintosh IIfx under System 7. Nothing to install. It starts in a couple of seconds and it saves where it always saved — inside the emulated Mac, which lives in your own browser.
launchNote: Boots straight to the title screen. Click through and pick a profession — banker is easy mode, farmer is hard mode with triple points.

macControls.does: Everything in the menus, the store and the map
Move the rifle sight while hunting

sections.h: How it works & what to expect
sections.html:
MachineMacintosh IIfx, 16 MB RAM, 640×480 at 256 colours
SystemSystem 7.5.3
EmulatorBasilisk II, compiled to WebAssembly
SoundYes — click once inside the screen first, browsers block audio until you do
SavesKept in your browser. Clearing site data wipes them.
MobilePlayable, but the hunting screen wants a real mouse

The emulator is a full Macintosh, not a re-implementation of the game, so what you get is exactly what shipped: the same fonts, the same slightly-too-slow dialogue boxes, the same music. The first load pulls a few megabytes of disk image; after that your browser has it cached and startup is close to instant.

sections.h: What you are actually playing
sections.html:
You start in Independence, Missouri, in the spring of 1848, and you have about two thousand miles to cover before the snow closes the Blue Mountains. First you pick a profession, and the choice is the whole difficulty setting: a banker from Boston starts with plenty of money and scores lowest, a carpenter from Ohio sits in the middle, and a farmer from Illinois starts poor and scores triple.

Then you spend at Matt's General Store — oxen, food, clothing, spare wagon parts, ammunition — and the first real lesson of the game is that you cannot afford everything and the thing you skipped is the thing that breaks.

After that it is a long, grinding series of small decisions. How fast to travel. How much to eat. Whether to ford a river, caulk the wagon and float it, or pay a ferryman you suspect is robbing you. Whether to spend three days hunting when you can only carry a hundred pounds of what you shoot. People in your party get cholera, measles, typhoid, a broken leg, and — famously — dysentery, and the game reports it in the same flat tone it uses for the weather.

It was written as a teaching tool and it never stopped being one. What it teaches, mostly, is that the frontier was a logistics problem and the logistics usually won.

sections.h: Why the Mac version is the one people remember
sections.html:
The Oregon Trail had a long life before this. It began in 1971 as a text game typed into a teletype by three student teachers in Minnesota, ran on the Apple II through the 1980s in that famous green monochrome, and got a DOS release in 1990 that most people call Oregon Trail Deluxe.

The 1991 Macintosh version is the one that ended up in the school computer lab, because the school computer lab in the 1990s was a room full of Macs. It has the colour art, the hunting mini-game with the animated bison, the tombstones you could write yourself, and the ending where the game scores you on how many of your family survived.

If your memory of the game is a black-and-white screen and a keyboard-only interface, you are remembering the Apple II. If it is colour, a mouse, and a bison you could never carry, you are remembering this.

faq.q: Is this the version I played at school?
faq.a: Almost certainly, if you were at school in the 1990s and the lab had Macintoshes. This is the 1991 MECC Macintosh release with colour graphics and the mouse-driven hunting screen. The green-on-black keyboard-only game is the earlier Apple II version, and the one with 3D wagons is Oregon Trail II from 1995.

faq.q: Do I need to install or download anything?
faq.a: No. The emulator is WebAssembly and runs inside the page. Nothing is installed on your computer and nothing you do is uploaded anywhere.

faq.q: Will my game be saved if I close the tab?
faq.a: Yes. Saves are written to the emulated Mac's hard disk, which is stored in your own browser. They survive closing the tab and restarting the computer. They do not survive clearing site data, and they do not follow you to another browser or another device.

faq.q: Why do I keep dying of dysentery?
faq.a: Dysentery in the game is driven mostly by how hard you are pushing the party: a grueling pace plus bare-bones rations plus bad weather is the combination that kills. Slow down to a steady pace and move to filling rations for a few days when someone gets ill, and rest when the game offers it.

faq.q: Should I ford the river or take the ferry?
faq.a: Check the depth first — the game tells you. Under about two and a half feet, fording is usually safe. Deeper than that and you are gambling your oxen, your food and sometimes a person against the ferry fee. Caulking and floating is the middle option and it is riskier than it sounds in a fast current.

faq.q: Can I play it on a phone?
faq.a: Yes, though it is fiddly. The menus and the store work fine with taps. The hunting screen expects a mouse you can move smoothly, and a touchscreen makes it much harder than it should be.

The game has not been sold in this form for more than twenty-five years and no rights holder distributes it. That is not the same as it being public domain, and this site does not pretend otherwise. There is a takedown page and a 48-hour promise behind it.

faq.q: Where can I get my own copy?
faq.a: The Internet Archive and Macintosh Garden both carry MECC's Macintosh releases. Both are linked below. If you would rather run your own file than ours, the loader on this site will take it.

title: Play Marathon (1994) Online — Bungie's Mac Shooter, Free & Legal
description: Bungie's Marathon, the Mac-only shooter that led to Halo, running free in your browser. Released for free redistribution by Bungie in 2005.
keywords: marathon 1994, play marathon online, bungie marathon, marathon mac, marathon durandal, marathon free
ogDescription: Bungie's Mac-only shooter, the one before Halo. Free and legal, running on an emulated Macintosh.
author: Bungie Software
fullyFree: Bungie authorised free redistribution of the whole Marathon trilogy in 2005 — not a shareware first chapter, the entire game.
licenseReason: Bungie released the Marathon trilogy for free redistribution in 2005 and has repeatedly blessed the community's continued distribution of it since, including the Aleph One bundles and the free Steam release. This is the original 1994 Macintosh build, not a port.
intro:
Before Halo, Bungie was a small Chicago company making games only for the Macintosh, and Marathon is the one that made their name. It came out in December 1994, six months after Doom shipped on DOS, and it did several things Doom did not: you could look up and down, the levels had real architecture, and — unusually for a shooter in 1994 — it had a plot worth reading.

This is the original Macintosh release running on an emulated Macintosh IIfx. Bungie put the whole trilogy into free redistribution in 2005, so there is nothing grey about it: the entire game is here, legally, at no cost.
launchNote: Boots to the Marathon title screen. Pick Begin New Game, then Total Carnage if you have played a shooter before — the default difficulty is gentle.

macControls.does: Action — open doors, use terminals, flip switches

sections.h: How it works & what to expect
sections.html:
MachineMacintosh IIfx, 32 MB RAM, 640×480 at 256 colours
SystemSystem 7.5.3
EmulatorBasilisk II, compiled to WebAssembly
SpeedComfortable on a desktop or laptop. A phone will struggle — this is the most demanding thing on the site.
SavesMarathon saves at pattern buffers inside the level; those saves live in your browser

Marathon ran on a 68040 Macintosh in 1994 and it wants roughly that much machine, which is a real ask for an interpreter running in a browser tab. On a modern desktop it is fine. On a phone it runs, but not at a framerate you would choose to fight in. Reduce the window size inside the game (the plus and minus keys) if it feels heavy.

sections.h: What Marathon actually is
sections.html:
You are a security officer aboard the UESC Marathon, a colony ship built out of the hollowed-out Martian moon Deimos, in orbit around Tau Ceti IV. An alien slave empire called the Pfhor attacks. That is the last simple sentence available about the plot.

What makes Marathon different is that the story is told through computer terminals scattered through the levels, and the three shipboard AIs talking to you through them do not agree with each other. Leela is helpful and straightforward. Durandal is rampant — a technical term in the game's fiction for an AI that has gone through anger and despair and out the other side into something like megalomania — and he is funny, unreliable, and by a distance the most memorable character in a 1994 shooter. Tycho is a third thing entirely.

Mechanically it holds up better than most of its generation. There is real verticality, oxygen management in vacuum levels, friendly BOBs you can accidentally shoot, dual-wielded pistols, and a physics model the community was modifying within months of release.

sections.h: The trilogy, and where to go next
sections.html:
Marathon (1994) was followed by Marathon 2: Durandal in 1995 — which added liquid you could swim in, better level design and a Windows 95 port, the first Bungie game most PC owners saw — and Marathon Infinity in 1996, which shipped with the level editor and a story that deliberately fractures.

All three are free. If you want them at a modern resolution with mouselook, the community engine Aleph One is the way: it is open source, actively maintained, and runs on everything. What you get here instead is the 1994 experience exactly as it shipped, keyboard turning and all.

And the lineage is not subtle. Read Durandal's terminals, then think about Cortana.

faq.a: Yes, and not in a wink-wink way. Bungie authorised free redistribution of the entire Marathon trilogy in 2005, has acknowledged the community's distribution of it repeatedly since, and the trilogy was published free on Steam in 2024 with Bungie's blessing.

faq.q: Is this the full game or a demo?
faq.a: The full game. All of Marathon, every level, not a shareware chapter.

faq.q: Why can't I look up and down with the mouse?
faq.a: Because it is 1994. Marathon does support mouse aiming, but the default configuration is keyboard turning, which is what most people used at the time. If you want modern controls, the Aleph One engine is the better route — it is linked below.

Same studio, and the connections are deliberate. The rampant AI Durandal is the clear ancestor of Cortana, several weapons and ideas carry over, and Bungie has always treated them as part of one lineage. Marathon is not set in the Halo universe, but it is unmistakably the same people.

faq.q: It runs slowly. What can I do?
faq.a: Shrink the game window with the minus key inside Marathon — it renders fewer pixels and the framerate jumps. Close other tabs. And use a desktop or laptop if you can: this is the heaviest title on the site.
At the pattern buffers — the glowing terminal-like devices inside levels. Marathon does not let you save anywhere you like, which takes some getting used to.

Born On Board — the civilian crew. They follow you, they shoot at the Pfhor, they are not very good at it, and they will absolutely walk into your line of fire. Shooting too many of them has consequences.

  • Original game data on GitHub — Bungie's files, preserved.

title: Play Kid Pix Online — The Original 1989 Mac Version, Free
description: Kid Pix as it first shipped: black and white, the dynamite eraser, the Wacky Brush and all the noises. Running free in your browser, no download.
keywords: kid pix online, kid pix 1.0, original kid pix, kid pix mac, kid pix free, kid pix browser
ogDescription: Craig Hickman's original, non-commercial Kid Pix — black and white, dynamite eraser, all the noises.
h1: Kid Pix, the 1989 original, in your browser
author: Craig Hickman
fullyFree: Craig Hickman released version 1.0 himself, free and non-commercial, before Brøderbund published the commercial version.
licenseReason: This is Kid Pix 1.0, the version Craig Hickman wrote for his son and released himself in 1989 as non-commercial software, before Brøderbund picked it up and published the commercial 1.1 in 1991. The later Brøderbund releases are not hosted here.
intro:
Craig Hickman wrote Kid Pix because he watched his three-year-old son try to use MacPaint and fail. Everything in MacPaint punished a mistake; nothing in it made a noise. So he built a drawing program where every tool was obvious, every action made a sound, and nothing you did could be wrong.

This is version 1.0 from 1989 — the one Hickman gave away himself, before Brøderbund published it commercially. It is black and white, it runs on an emulated Mac Plus, and it is the fastest thing on this site: the whole machine is 512 by 342 pixels and starts instantly.
launchNote: Opens straight into a blank page with the toolbar down the left. Try the stick of dynamite in the eraser menu.

macControls.does: Draw, and pick tools from the palette on the left
Opens that tool's variations along the bottom
Undo — although the eraser is more fun
Save your picture inside the emulated Mac

sections.h: How it works & what to expect
sections.html:
MachineMacintosh Plus, 4 MB RAM, 512×342 black and white
SystemSystem 6.0.8
EmulatorMini vMac, compiled to WebAssembly
SpeedInstant. This runs comfortably on a phone.
SoundYes, and the sounds are half the point. Click inside the screen once to let the browser play audio.

A Mac Plus is a tiny machine by any modern measure — eight megahertz, one megabyte of RAM as standard — which is why this is the lightest emulation on the site. It is also why the screen is black and white and rather small. That is not a limitation of the emulator; that was the computer.

sections.h: The tools worth finding
sections.html:
Kid Pix's design principle was that a child should be able to discover everything by poking at it, so the descriptions below are slightly against the spirit of the thing. Poke at it first.

  • The Wacky Brush. Not one brush — a menu of them. Bubbles, dripping paint, a trail of little shapes, echoes of whatever you last drew.
  • The stick of dynamite. One of the erasers. It blows the whole picture up, with a bang.
  • The rubber stamps. A tray of small black-and-white icons — animals, vehicles, faces — that you stamp anywhere.
  • The Electric Mixer. Takes whatever is on the page and scrambles it, in one of several increasingly alarming ways.
  • The letter stamps. Type and each letter arrives with a sound.

Everything makes a noise. The pencil squeaks, the paint can splats, the eraser goes whoosh. Hickman recorded a lot of these himself.

sections.h: What happened next
sections.html:
Brøderbund published Kid Pix commercially in 1991 and it became one of the best-selling pieces of educational software of the decade. Kid Pix Companion followed in 1992 with the slideshow feature, then Kid Pix 2 in 1994 brought colour, and the line continued under Brøderbund, The Learning Company and Riverdeep for years afterwards.

The version here is the one before all of that: Hickman's own release, black and white, with the sounds he recorded and the tools he chose. Plenty of people who loved Kid Pix as children have never seen it. It holds up remarkably well, partly because a program built so that a three-year-old cannot get it wrong turns out to be a pleasant thing for an adult too.

faq.q: Is this the Kid Pix I remember?
faq.a: If you remember colour, it is not — you are remembering Kid Pix 2 from 1994 or later. This is the original 1989 black-and-white version, which is the direct ancestor: same tools, same sounds, same dynamite.
Yes. Craig Hickman released version 1.0 himself as non-commercial software before Brøderbund published the commercial version. The later Brøderbund releases are not hosted here.

faq.q: Why is it black and white?
faq.a: Because the Macintosh Plus it was written for was black and white. Colour Macs existed in 1989 but were expensive, and Kid Pix was built to run on the cheap machine a school or a family actually had.

faq.q: Can I save or print my picture?
faq.a: You can save it inside the emulated Mac and it will still be there next time. Getting it out to a real file on your computer is not wired up yet — it is on the list.

faq.q: Does it work on a phone or tablet?
faq.a: Yes, and better than most things here. The emulated machine is small and simple, and drawing with a finger turns out to suit it.

Craig Hickman, an art professor at the University of Oregon, who wrote it for his son Ben after watching him struggle with MacPaint. He has said the core idea was that a drawing program for a small child should have no wrong moves.

intro:
In 1989 Berkeley Systems shipped a utility that stopped your monitor from burning an image into its phosphor. In 1991 they added a module in which chrome toasters with flapping wings fly slowly across the screen accompanied by slices of toast, and that module became one of the most recognisable pieces of software of the decade.

This is the real After Dark on a real emulated Macintosh, not a web re-creation. You get the control panel, the module list, the sliders, and the toasters as Berkeley Systems drew them.

After Dark was not an application — it was a system extension and a control panel, which is why it needs a whole Macintosh around it rather than being something you could port to a web page. That is also why running it here means booting System 7 first. It takes a couple of seconds.

sections.h: The modules worth your time
sections.html:
• Flying Toasters. The famous one. Chrome toasters, flapping wings, slices of toast, and a slider for how many.
  • Fish! An aquarium. Berkeley Systems' first hit module and, for a lot of offices, the reason After Dark got bought.
  • Mowin' Man. A small man mows your screen. When he finishes, it grows back.
  • Warp. Stars streaking past. Simple, and the one that looked best on a big monitor.
  • Boris. A cat that walks across your screen, and later got a whole product to himself.
  • Rainstorm. Rain down the glass with thunder. Genuinely calming, thirty-five years on.

There is also a Randomizer, which cycles modules, and a MultiModule that runs several at once — which on a 1991 Macintosh was showing off.

sections.h: Why a screensaver mattered
sections.html:
The original justification was technical and real. Cathode-ray tubes with a static image left on them for weeks would retain a ghost of it permanently, and in an office full of terminals showing the same spreadsheet all day, that was a genuine hardware problem.

What Berkeley Systems worked out is that the fix could be entertainment. A screensaver is a piece of software with no job to do and complete freedom over the screen, running in an era when almost every other program was a grid of grey boxes. After Dark was one of the first pieces of software people bought for pleasure rather than for a task, and the toasters ended up on t-shirts, mugs and a lawsuit with Jefferson Airplane over whose flying toasters came first.

LCD panels do not burn in the way CRTs did, so the technical reason evaporated. The toasters outlived it comfortably.

faq.q: Is this the real After Dark or a web imitation?
faq.a: The real software. There are many Flying Toasters tributes built in CSS, JavaScript or as modern screensavers; this is Berkeley Systems' actual Macintosh release running inside an emulated Macintosh, control panel and all.
The Macintosh After Dark from the early 1990s, the version whose module set includes Flying Toasters, Fish!, Mowin' Man, Warp and Boris.

faq.q: Can I use it as my actual screensaver?
faq.a: No — it runs inside the emulated Mac, in a browser tab, so it has no way to take over your real screen. What you get is the thing itself, on demand.

faq.q: Why does it need a whole emulated Macintosh?
faq.a: Because After Dark was a system extension, not an application. It hooked into the Mac OS to take over the screen when the machine went idle, which means it only exists in the context of a running Mac OS.

It is genuinely murky. Berkeley Systems was acquired in the late 1990s and the After Dark name has changed hands more than once since, but nobody has sold the Macintosh version in decades. If you hold the rights, the takedown page is linked in the footer.

faq.q: Were the Flying Toasters stolen from Jefferson Airplane?
faq.a: Jefferson Airplane sued over it in 1994, pointing at the cover of their 1973 album Thirty Seconds Over Winterland, which has flying toasters on it. The case did not go the band's way.

intro:
You are a paper aeroplane. You are indoors. Gravity is pulling you down and the only thing keeping you up is the hot air coming out of the heating vents, so the whole game is a slow negotiation with a house that is full of candles, drips, rubber bands and a cat.

Glider PRO is the 1994 peak of a series John Calhoun had been refining since 1988, and in 2016 he put the whole thing — code and art — on GitHub under the GPL. It is free in every sense.

If you want Glider PRO at a modern resolution with gamepad support and the level editor, there is a maintained port called Aerofoil built on Calhoun's released source. It is the better way to play seriously. What is here is the original, as it shipped.

sections.h: The house, and everything in it
sections.html:
Each room is a single screen and the glider drifts through it left to right, or right to left, or up through a hole in the ceiling. The furniture is the level design:

  • Heating vents and air ducts. Your engine. Hover over one to climb; the entire skill of the game is learning to ride them.
  • Candles. Fly through the flame and the paper burns. Obviously.
  • Drips and steam. Wet paper does not fly.
  • Rubber bands and paper clips. Fired at you by things that resent your presence.
  • The cat. A problem.
  • Batteries, helium, and the paper aeroplane power-ups. Temporary thrust, temporary lift, and extra lives.

Glider PRO shipped with several houses and a built-in editor, and the community built hundreds more. That editor is the reason the game is still alive: there is far more Glider content made by players than by Casady & Greene.

sections.h: Why it was freed
sections.html:
John Calhoun wrote the first Glider in 1988 as shareware, and the series ran through Glider 3.1.4 and Glider 4.0 before Casady & Greene published Glider PRO commercially in 1994. Casady & Greene closed in 2003.

In 2016 Calhoun put the complete source on GitHub under the GPL — the Macintosh Programmer's Workshop project files, the resource forks, the artwork, everything. That is rarer than it sounds. Most Macintosh games of that era are stuck in limbo because the publisher dissolved and nobody is sure who inherited what. Glider PRO is simply free, because the person who wrote it decided it should be.

faq.q: Why can I not just click Play here?
faq.a: Because it does not work yet, and a button that says Play should mean it. Glider PRO boots on our emulated Mac and reaches its title screen, but then reports “there are no houses on this drive” — it cannot find the level files that sit right beside it. The files are present and byte-identical to the distribution, so the fault is in how the disk image is assembled rather than in the game. Until that is fixed this page runs a copy you supply, and the maintained Aerofoil port is the better way to play Glider PRO today in any case.
Yes, genuinely. John Calhoun released the source code and the game assets on GitHub in 2016 under the GNU GPL version 2.

Get the paper aeroplane through the house to the end without burning, soaking or shredding it. Later houses add doors you have to find keys for and rooms that only open once you have done something elsewhere.

faq.q: How do I stay in the air?
faq.a: Ride the updrafts. The vents and ducts blow upward — position yourself over one and you rise. Most deaths are from trying to cross a room with no lift in it.

faq.q: Can I build my own houses?
faq.a: Glider PRO shipped with a level editor and it is in this version. The modern Aerofoil port has a better one and can import the hundreds of houses the community made.

faq.q: Should I play this or Aerofoil?
faq.a: Aerofoil if you want to play a lot of it — modern resolution, gamepad support, the community houses. This one if you want the 1994 game exactly as it was, in one click, with nothing installed.
Several. Glider 4.0 from 1991 is the direct predecessor and Calhoun released its source too. It is simpler, black and white, and charming in its own right.

A year after Marathon, Bungie did what sequels rarely do and improved nearly everything. Marathon 2 added water and lava you could swim through, vastly better level architecture, friendly aliens, and a structure that sends you back and forth across the surface of Lh'owon rather than around one ship.

It is also the first Bungie game most people outside the Macintosh world ever saw: a Windows 95 port followed in 1996. This is the original Mac release.

Marathon 2 is slightly heavier than the first game because there is more going on in each room. If it feels sluggish, shrink the game window with the minus key — it renders fewer pixels and the framerate jumps immediately.

sections.h: What changed from Marathon
sections.html:
The obvious addition is liquid. Marathon 2 lets you swim, and it uses that for whole levels of underwater navigation and for lava you have to cross quickly. It sounds small; it changes the shape of the level design completely.

Less obvious but more important: the levels are better. The first Marathon was corridors in a spaceship, which is what 1994 shooters were. Marathon 2 is set on a planet, with outdoor spaces, ruined architecture and rooms that look like places rather than arenas.

There are also allies. The S'pht'Kr fight alongside you, and the game is careful to make you notice when they die. Durandal is still in charge, still rampant, still funnier than a computer in a shooter has any right to be, and considerably more open about the fact that he is using you.

sections.h: The Windows port, and why it matters
sections.html:
Bungie shipped Marathon 2 for Windows 95 in 1996 under the name Marathon 2: Durandal. It did not sell especially well against Quake, which arrived the same year, but it is the hinge between Bungie the Mac developer and Bungie the studio Microsoft bought in 2000.

If you want to play seriously, the Aleph One engine gives you all three games at a modern resolution with mouselook. What is here is the 1995 Macintosh release exactly as it shipped.

intro:
Marathon Infinity is the one where the story stops behaving. You die, and wake up somewhere earlier. You change sides. Whole chapters turn out to be something other than what they appeared. It is a 1996 first-person shooter structured like a short story that folds back on itself, and it should not work as well as it does.

sections.h: The branching that is not branching
sections.html:
Infinity presents itself as a story with alternative paths, and the trick is that your choices are not what move you between them — dying is. Fail in particular ways and the game does not simply reload; it continues somewhere else, in a different version of events, sometimes on a different side of the war.

Because of that, the level list is not the story order, and two people who finish Infinity will describe different games. In 1996 this was genuinely novel and there was no walkthrough to spoil it.

It is also the hardest of the three by some distance. If you want the trilogy's best-paced game, that is Marathon 2. Infinity is the one to play afterwards, when you want it to be strange.

sections.h: Forge, Anvil, and why Marathon never died
sections.html:
Bungie shipped Infinity with its own tools: Forge for building levels and Anvil for editing the sprites, sounds and physics. Nothing else in 1996 handed you the editors the developers had used, and the result was a modding community that produced hundreds of complete total conversions — some of them, like the Eternal and Rubicon projects, larger than the games they were built on.

That community is why all three games still run on modern machines through the Aleph One engine, which grew out of the Marathon 2 source Bungie released in 2000.

sections.h: What is different from Glider PRO
sections.html:
Glider PRO, three years later, added colour, much larger houses, a level editor and a great deal of furniture. Glider 4.0 is smaller and purer: one house, one idea, black and white, and it is over quickly enough to play through in a sitting.

Because it targets a Macintosh Plus rather than a Quadra, it is also the version that runs best on modest hardware — including a phone. If you have never played any Glider, this is a good place to start and it costs you nothing to find out.

sections.h: Shareware, and what that meant
sections.html:
Glider was shareware: you got the whole game, and if you liked it you sent the author money. That model carried an enormous share of Macintosh software through the late 1980s and early 1990s, distributed on bulletin boards, on disks passed around user groups, and later on the Info-Mac archive.

It also produced a strange kind of authorship. A shareware game had one name on it, usually a person rather than a company, and the registration notice often included their home address. John Calhoun was one of that generation who kept going: Glider ran from 1988 to 1994 through four major versions, ended up published commercially by Casady & Greene, and was eventually released as open source by the same person who started it.

intro:
In January 1984 almost nobody had used a mouse. MacPaint is the program that explained it. You pick up a brush, you drag, and paint appears — obvious now, astonishing then, and the single most effective demonstration Apple had of why a Macintosh was different from everything else on a desk.

Bill Atkinson wrote it, and it is a remarkable piece of engineering as well as a remarkable piece of design: full-page bitmap editing with smooth interactive dragging, on a machine with 128 kilobytes of memory.

Black and white is not a limitation of the emulation; the Macintosh had no colour until 1987, and MacPaint's entire visual vocabulary — the fifty-ish fill patterns along the bottom of the window — exists because black and white was all there was.

sections.h: What to try
sections.html:
• The fill patterns. Double-click one to edit it. A pattern editor, in 1984, in 128K.
  • The lasso versus the marquee. The lasso shrinks to fit whatever you drew; the marquee takes a rectangle. Atkinson wrote the lasso because a rectangle was the wrong selection for a drawing.
  • FatBits. Zoom to individual pixels while a small inset shows the drawing at normal size. Still the right design.
  • The spray can and the paint bucket. Both arrived here first for most people who ever used them.

sections.h: Why it mattered
sections.html:
MacPaint shipped free with every Macintosh, alongside MacWrite, because a computer with a graphical interface and nothing graphical to do would have been a hard sell. It was written in Pascal and assembly and fitted into a machine with no hard disk, and the interactive performance it achieved on that hardware is the part programmers still find impressive.

Apple donated the source code to the Computer History Museum in 2010, and it can be read there. Almost every raster graphics program since owes it something: the tool palette down the left, the marquee, the lasso, the pixel zoom, the pattern fill. Photoshop's interface is a direct descendant.

Kid Pix, also on this site, was written explicitly as a reaction to it — Craig Hickman watched his three-year-old fail to use MacPaint and built something with no wrong moves.

intro: A grid of numbers. A small green creature with a large mouth. A prompt at the top telling you to eat the multiples of seven, and four Troggles wandering in to eat you instead. Number Munchers is a maths drill dressed as an arcade game, and it is one of the few educational programs that children played voluntarily.

sections.h: The modes, and which one is hardest
sections.html:
• Multiples. Eat every multiple of the given number. The gentlest mode and the one everyone remembers.
  • Factors. Eat the factors of the given number. Genuinely harder, because it requires you to think in the other direction.
  • Primes. Eat the prime numbers. Fine until the grid fills with numbers in the eighties and nineties.
  • Equality and Inequality. Eat the expressions that equal — or do not equal — the target. The ones that turn a maths drill into a reading-speed test.

The Troggles are the pressure. They enter from the edges, move on their own schedule, and several varieties behave differently — some follow the grid, some cut across it, some eat numbers themselves and change the board under you.

sections.h: Why MECC's games worked
sections.html:
The Minnesota Educational Computing Consortium was a state-funded body set up to put computers into Minnesota's schools, and it ended up making some of the most widely played software of the 1980s and 1990s almost by accident. The Oregon Trail is the famous one, but Number Munchers, Word Munchers, Odell Lake and Fraction Munchers were on every lab machine in North America.

What they got right was that the education had to be the mechanic rather than a reward attached to one. You do not answer a maths question to earn a turn at a game; eating the right number is the game, and the Troggle closing in is what makes you answer quickly. That is a harder design problem than it looks, and most educational software since has failed it.
